chapter: Dana Valery and the Glenn Miller band
title: Back home: twin sons, Three Rivers Inn and playing bass for singers
summary: He returns to the US, works at the Three Rivers Inn in Syracuse, and plays bass behind Billy Eckstine with Charlie Persip.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Well an occupation — well it wasn’t an occupation of course because we were not occupying that country. It was the Republic of South Korea. In fact there’s still about 20 or 30 thousand guys over there. There was 50 thousand then. But it was an absolute wild time I’ll tell you that. And then I wound up delivering my own twin sons there, but I couldn’t get them out because I didn’t have enough time to get married and do the paperwork, and then I finally got transferred back to America. And when I got home I threw it on the floor and I said to my parents, I said, “well there’s your grandchildren.” A picture of them. I think my mother looked at it and said, “you’re going back aren’t you?” And I said, “yeah, I’m going to go get them.” But I had to figure out how to get there. So it took two years, so I worked at Three Rivers Inn in Syracuse. And then we did the — I got that job and my reading had improved and I got that job playing like Frankie Laine, and I can’t remember all the people who came in but the various acts. But I played a session on bass one night with some guys and there was no bass player so I just started playing bass. So I said, “well I’ll play bass in the band, that’s fine with me.” So I got to play with Billy Eckstine and the drummer was Charlie Persip. Here I’m playing bass with Charlie Persip who is one of my favorite big band drummers from Dizzy Gillespie’s big band. That’s another record that I was kind of weaned on, “Dizzy at Newport.” Here’s I’m playing bass with Charlie Persip playing drums. Patti Page — I played the bass on that show. I wound up playing bass the second time on the Frankie Laine show. We called it the Frankly Lame show.
